title: Soft-landing pause and work-resuming resume for track A (cutoff word, age-based landing, pause manifest)
body:
## Problem

Every pause so far has been a hard landing. The 2026-09-12 chain (`/tmp/owner-pause-v2.sh` then `/tmp/final-pause.sh`) set the caps to 0, killed the waiting dispatches and, at the deadline, SIGTERMed every codex worker and lane: 17 sessions died mid-work. PR #552's `results/telemetry/owner-tools/owner-pause.sh` fixes the hygiene (admission stops first, waiters release themselves on `watchdog/drain`, crontab backed up, one `pause-state.json`, idempotent caps) but keeps the same landing: at deadline −2:00 it kills every leftover worker, and `owner-resume.sh` restores caps and daemons, not the work.

Cost of a kill: a codex session has already paid for its input and reasoning; only its rollout survives, so restarting it on resume pays everything again. The fallout seen on 2026-09-14: reviewers that "exited 143", kill-caused `daemon/prN.failed` markers that made the daemon skip PRs for two hours after resume, a worktree left in an abandoned merge, and every lane restarted from scratch (CI and a full review redone on heads that already carried both statuses).

Owner instruction (2026-09-14): "I allow 15 minutes to do the pause ... there should be a better way to pause the development, whether for slow mode or for full speed mode, than hard landing. The current way is not resume-friendly and may cause quota waste."

## Requirements (soft landing, on top of PR #552's tooling)

1. **Two owner words.** `owner-pause.sh --cutoff` stops admission only (caps to 0, `watchdog/drain`, waiters release themselves, no kill, daemons keep running so finished work still merges) and may be given long before the pause. `owner-pause.sh` (the pause word) starts the deadline landing from `run.pause_deadline_min`. A pause without a prior cutoff degrades gracefully to rule 2.
2. **Age-based landing instead of a blanket kill.** At the pause word every running codex session is classified by role and elapsed time (registry row / process start): young sessions (little sunk cost) are stopped at once; mature reviewers run until the last minute because they usually finish; provers that cannot finish are checkpointed (their worktree stays as is, their codex thread id, worktree, step and elapsed time are recorded) and stopped only at the last minute. Thresholds live in the run brief / `local/capacity-policy.json`, never as literals in the script.
3. **A pause manifest that records the work, not only the caps.** `watchdog/pause-state.json` (the single record `owner-resume.sh` reads) gains: per lane the issue, branch, head sha, the step reached and the statuses already present on the head; per stopped session the thread id, role, worktree, elapsed time and whether it is resumable; the failed markers created by the landing.
4. **Resume the work.** `owner-resume.sh` (after restoring caps and daemons as today) relaunches parked lanes at the step they reached: skip the merge/build/push when the head is unchanged, skip CI and review when the head already carries `local-ci/summary` / `local-review/summary` success; resumes stopped provers with `codex exec resume <thread> "<continue prompt>"` through `dispatch.sh --resume` (codex-cli 0.153.4 supports `exec resume`; `dispatch.sh` in #552 already takes `--resume THREAD_ID` and `--continue-from`); restarts stopped reviewers from scratch (a resumed review re-reads its whole context, so a restart is not cheaper only when the review was nearly done, which rule 2 already lets finish); clears the kill-caused failed markers it recorded.
5. **Provers commit at milestones.** The prover dispatch prompt / persona gains the rule "commit each proved lemma in the worktree (hooks run) before starting the next"; a kill then loses at most the work since the last commit, and the resume prompt tells the prover to continue from the worktree state.
6. **Tests and protocol.** `scripts/tests/` covers the classification, the manifest round trip and the step skipping (no live codex, no network); `local/protocols/full-speed-mode.md` §6 and the owner-tools README describe the two words, the landing rules and the resume behaviour; AGENTS.md only if an agent-facing rule changes.

Out of scope here (separate follow-up): probing a key before assignment and retiring it on the first 429/403 (touches the accounts/capacity work of #555 / PR #556).

## Acceptance

- `owner-pause.sh --dry-run` prints the phase plan with the classification rule and the recorded thresholds; `--cutoff` touches no process.
- A simulated landing (fixture registry rows and fake pids) stops the young sessions, keeps the mature ones, records the provers as resumable in `pause-state.json`, and a simulated resume relaunches each recorded lane at the right step and issues the right `dispatch.sh --resume` calls (asserted, not executed).
- No literal timestamp, cap, issue number or deadline in the scripts (#552's rule); every commit within the 1000-line scaffolding budget (no override); CI green; an independent review approved.
- Branch stacked on `issue-550-full-speed-v2` (PR #552), like #554 and #556.

labels.name: infrastructure
labels.description: Foundational definitions, shared APIs, or supporting layers

body:
<!-- mipstarre-issue-key: merge-title-lean-loc-20260914 -->
### Request

Owner request, 2026-09-14: every merge commit the pipeline creates should carry, in its
**title**, the number of Lean lines the merged PR changed, so the GitHub commits page shows
the size of each packet without opening the merge.

### Format

The merge title becomes:

    Merge PR #N: <PR title> [lean +A -D]

where A and D are added and deleted lines in `*.lean` files, summed over
`git diff --numstat <merge-base>...<head> -- '*.lean'`. A PR that touches no Lean file gets
`[lean 0]`. The PR title is truncated to roughly 80 characters so the subject stays readable.
A one-line body names the frozen head SHA.

### Scope

`gh_common.merge_pr` gains optional `commit_title` / `commit_message` parameters, forwarded
as the REST merge payload keys of the same names and omitted entirely when None, so existing
callers keep GitHub's default title. `pr_merge.py` computes the delta just before merging and
passes the title. The exact-head `sha` guard and the merge-commit topology verification are
untouched.

### Accuracy

Approximate is fine. The count is a size signal for the commits page, not an audited figure:
it is taken from the local merge base, ignores rename detection subtleties, and falls back to
omitting the bracket (GitHub's default title) if the git computation fails for any reason.
The merge itself must never fail because the count could not be produced.

title: Hot-editable accounts file: keys, ceilings and health without owner prompts

labels.name: infrastructure
labels.description: Foundational definitions, shared APIs, or supporting layers

body:
<!-- mipstarre-issue-key: qpbt-accounts-file -->
## Motivation

The owner's real capacity is not a fact of the run; it changes during it. There are one to
three endpoints, each with one or two API keys, and each key has a concurrency limit
somewhere between 5 and 40 that moves while work is going on: the endpoint admin
reassigns slots away, the owner wins them back, a key becomes invalid, a key runs out of
quota. On 2026-09-12 that reality reached the pipeline only as messages — the limits were
restated five times and the caps were edited by hand ten times — and the messages had to
be typed to a session, which had to be idle to receive them.

The run brief (#550, work item W1) fixed the *start* of a run: one artifact states the
keys and their ceilings, and `run_mode.py apply` turns it into the mode file. It did not
fix the *middle* of a run. The brief is one-shot by design; changing a ceiling today means
re-applying a brief, which re-seeds every derived value, and nothing at all lets the owner
add or retire a key. Worse, two key names are hard-coded through the layer —
`account_router.ACCOUNTS = ("primary", "second")`, `run_mode.ACCOUNT_NAMES`,
`dispatch.sh`'s `for account in primary second`, the `--account` choices — so a third key
cannot be expressed at all, and the second key's `CODEX_HOME` is a special case in
`dispatch.sh` rather than a field.

This issue makes the set of usable keys and their ceilings a **live, owner-owned file**
that the running pipeline re-reads, editable from a shell or from GitHub, with no prompt
to the meta session and no re-brief.

## Description

Agreed with the owner on 2026-09-12; six points.

1. **One live file.** `~/.cache/mipstarre-dev/watchdog/accounts.json` is the source of
   truth: a list of `{name, label, endpoint, codex_home, ceiling, external_reserved,
   enabled, note}`, one entry per key, any number of endpoints and keys. **Key values
   never appear in it** — they live in the codex home the entry points at, which only the
   owner touches. The brief's `accounts` block becomes the INITIAL content:
   `run_mode.py apply` writes the file when it is absent and **never overwrites an
   existing one**, so the brief stays one-shot while the accounts file is live.

2. **Re-read every tick, with ceiling semantics.** The capacity controller and
   `account_router.py` re-read the file on every tick and every reservation (at most 60 s
   stale). `ceiling` is a ceiling, never a target: below it the AIMD discovery is
   unchanged (multiplicative decrease on refusals, additive increase while refusals are
   zero, up to `ceiling - external_reserved`). Lowering the ceiling takes effect at the
   next tick; raising it lets the additive creep continue. `enabled: false` means cap 0
   immediately and no probes; removing an entry means the same.

3. **Measured health.** Live-session failures are classified per key —
   `401`/`403`/invalid key, `INSUFFICIENT_BALANCE`, sustained 5xx — and a key that trips
   is disabled automatically with a **reason**, recorded in
   `watchdog/capacity/health.json` (one document for every key, next to the existing
   per-account files). While it is disabled a cheap read-only probe every N minutes
   re-enables it when it succeeds. The owner sees the state on the hourly readiness
   report: one line per key with ceiling, effective cap, live, refusals in the last ten
   minutes, health and note.

4. **Two owner touchpoints, neither of them a prompt.**
   (a) `results/telemetry/owner-tools/accounts.sh list | get | set <name> <field> <value> |
   enable <name> | disable <name> | add <name> --endpoint --codex-home --ceiling |
   remove <name> | probe [name]` validates and writes the file atomically (temp file +
   rename) and appends one line to `watchdog/capacity/accounts.log`.
   (b) A GitHub channel for when the owner is away from a shell: a comment on the owner
   inbox issue in the fixed form `ACCOUNTS: <name> ceiling=<n> [reserved=<n>]
   [enabled=true|false]` (one or more per comment), applied by the janitor at its next
   sweep **only when the comment author is the repository owner login**, and echoed back
   with a confirmation reply (`applied: …` or `rejected: …`) so the owner knows it took
   effect.

5. **N named accounts.** The router, the controller, `dispatch.sh --account`, the lane
   slot counting and the pause/resume caps snapshot handle any number of named accounts;
   no code path enumerates `primary` and `second`. Those two names keep working as
   ordinary entries, so every existing brief, cap file and session row is unchanged.

6. **Documentation.** The runbook section in `local/protocols/full-speed-mode.md` and the
   owner-tools README: how to edit the file, the CLI, the inbox comment form, and what the
   hourly per-key line means.

## Testing

`scripts/tests/test_accounts_file.py`, `test_accounts_hot_reload.py`,
`test_accounts_inbox.py` and `test_accounts_router_n.py` under the existing
`python3 -m unittest discover -s scripts/tests -p 'test_*.py'` step, all runnable without
any

title: chsh build farm: offload Lean builds to chsh in full speed mode only

labels.name: infrastructure

<!-- mipstarre-issue-key: qpbt-chsh-build-farm -->
<!-- mipstarre-issue-key: qpbt-chsh-build-farm -->
## Motivation

The 2026-09-12 full speed run was CPU-bound on ghz: 128 cores shared with other users,
load 90-150 for four hours, a median CI build of 61 s and lane builds queueing behind the
machine-wide full-build lease. A second host is now prepared and idle. `chsh` (192 cores,
2 TB RAM, aarch64, ZFS with 10 TB free) carries a byte-identical copy of the Mathlib
package cache, the same Lean 4.32.0 toolchain, a hardlink build seed and a checkout that
mirrors ghz. The link from ghz measures 86.7 MB/s; a cold lane offload took 14.9 s and a
one-file rebuild 17.2 s round trip, against a 19-minute full warm build.

Nothing is wired today. The offload script exists only as a draft outside the repository,
the mode layer has no field that says whether a run may use the second host, and a lane
that tried would fail whenever chsh was unreachable. This issue makes the build farm a
*mode* of the run rather than an operator action.

## The owner rule

**chsh is used only in full speed mode, and never otherwise.** In full speed mode the
compute and the storage of chsh are used alongside ghz; outside it the pipeline must not
contact chsh at all. The offload is therefore a function of the run mode alone, false by
default and false after a pause — not a switch an operator flips and forgets.

**No codex on chsh, and none is to be installed.** chsh's own internet is about 16 KB/s;
it is a pure build node fed from ghz by rsync. No worker session, no dispatch, no review
ever runs there.

## Description

1. **The mode field.** `run.compute.offload_hosts` in the run brief (for example
   `["chsh"]`), validated by `local/bin/run_mode.py` against the known hosts.
   `run_mode.py get offload` answers `yes` only when `run.speed` is `fast` **and** the
   host is listed **and** the run is not paused; every other case is `no`. An absent
   `run.compute` is `no`. Nothing else decides this question.

2. **The offload script.** `results/telemetry/owner-tools/build-on-chsh.sh`, a versioned
   and hardened copy of the draft: `BatchMode` ssh over the internal address
   (`HostName 192.168.1.18`, port 22) with a known-hosts file the installer places at
   `~/.cache/mipstarre-dev/watchdog/chsh/known_hosts`; one `flock` per lane; a toolchain
   equality check; the six steps of the design (push sources, hardlink seed, shared
   package symlink, `lake build`, return only the artifacts the build wrote, exit with
   lake's code); a distinct exit code for "chsh is unusable" so a caller can tell a
   transport failure from a failed proof; `--dry-run`, which prints every command and
   contacts chsh not at all; and one line per build in
   `~/.cache/mipstarre-dev/watchdog/chsh/offload.log` naming the host that built.

3. **Lanes and CI use it, and never depend on it.** `local/bin/lane.sh` and
   `local/bin/ci.sh` take their `lake build` steps through the offload when the mode says
   `yes`, and **fall back to the local build on any ssh or rsync failure**. A lane must
   never fail because chsh is unreachable, and the log must always say which host built.
   A genuinely failing build is passed through, never retried locally in the hope of a
   different answer. The pre-push per-file `lake env lean` gate stays on ghz.

4. **The seed refresh.** When main moves, chsh's checkout and its hardlink seed go stale
   and a lane rebuilds the difference — slow, never wrong. The merge daemon triggers a
   detached, locked refresh after a merge, rate-limited to at most one an hour and only
   while the offload is enabled.

5. **Installation.** `results/telemetry/owner-tools/install.sh` deploys the script under
   its hash manifest and installs the known-hosts file. Nothing is installed on chsh.

6. **Runbook.** `local/protocols/full-speed-mode.md`: what chsh is, the rule, how to
   verify that it was used, and what to do when chsh is down — nothing, the fallback is
   automatic.

## Acceptance

- `run_mode.py get offload` is `no` for a default-speed brief, `no` for a fast brief that
  does not list the host, `no` after `run_mode.py pause`, and `yes` only for a fast,
  unpaused brief listing chsh; an unknown host in the brief is an exit-2 validation error.
- `build-on-chsh.sh --dry-run <worktree>` prints the rsync and ssh command lines and makes
  no network call.
- With ssh failing, the lane and CI build helper falls back to the local build, returns
  the local build's exit code and logs `host=ghz`.
- `bash -n` on the changed shell files and the unit suite
  (`python3 -m unittest discover -s scripts/tests -p 'test_*.py'`) pass.

Follow-up to the full speed mode v2 tracker #550; the branch is stacked on
`issue-550-full-speed-v2`.

<!-- mipstarre-issue-key: qpbt-full-speed-v2 -->
## Motivation

The full speed run of 2026-09-12 (04:17Z–08:33Z) produced 9 merges and cost the owner
eight distinct classes of manual intervention, each of which is a defect of the workflow
(`results/telemetry/owner-handoffs/2026-09-12-main.md`, the `## 2026-09-12` sections of the
event log, and the run summary). The owner had to restate the concurrency limits five
times while ~90 worker sessions died (69 on a dead endpoint, the rest above an unmeasured
provider ceiling); ask repeatedly why slots were idle while every dispatched fixer was
dying at a model-policy preflight; ask whether the project was progressing and then
dictate the estimate format; ask why ready PRs were not merging; watch three lane-runner
revisions be hand-patched in `/tmp`; switch the speed tier three times by hand; and nudge
a main session whose message-delivery script auto-resumed the goal five minutes after the
stop order.

The target state: the owner gives **one** briefing at the start of a run (keys and their
limits, duration or "until my word", speed tier, pause deadline) and afterwards receives
only the half-hourly one-line estimate on the estimate issue and prose progress on the
progress log. Everything else is an automatic mechanism, a one-file switch, or a
self-healing loop, and every fix lives in the repository rather than in `/tmp`.

Design document: attached as the first comment on this issue, which is the brief of
record; the per-item briefs land in `local/briefs/`.

## Description

Seven work items, disjoint file sets, each one reviewed PR closing one sub-issue of this
tracker.

1. **Owner briefing, run-mode and standing reports.** `local/bin/run_mode.py` validates
   one `run-brief.json` and is the only writer of `watchdog/run-mode.json` and of the
   derived cap files; `ready_report.py` answers "ready but open, and why" hourly on the
   progress log; `estimate_post.py` is the single writer of the estimate issue and renders
   exactly the two prescribed lines. The main persona gains a Standing reports section so
   the closing report is a duty, not a pause-message dictation.
2. **Dispatch and telemetry.** Provider failures are classified (`concurrency_limit`,
   `endpoint_5xx`, `retries_exhausted`, `timeout`, `task_failure`, `unknown`) and recorded
   with the endpoint, so a capacity refusal is no longer indistinguishable from a failed
   proof; `dispatch.sh` spools its request and retries transient classes instead of dying
   with its prompt; a branch claim stops two writers on one worktree; an owner model
   override lives in the policy layer instead of a PATH-shim rewrite that made the session
   registry record the wrong model; `autofix.sh` stops defaulting to a model its own
   preflight rejects and gains the fix → CI → review loop that lived in `/tmp`.
3. **Capacity controller.** An AIMD controller with per-endpoint health is the only writer
